title: REHOBOAM HAD EIGHTEEN WIVES AND SIXTY CONCUBINES—But Loved One Woman More Than All the Others
paragraphs: REHOBOAM HAD EIGHTEEN WIVES AND SIXTY CONCUBINES—But Loved One Woman More Than All the Others

He had access to more women than most men could imagine. Yet Scripture quietly records that one woman held a place the others did not—and hidden inside that uncomfortable story is a warning about desire, favoritism, legacy, and the things we think will finally satisfy us.
And still, in the middle of all those staggering numbers, Scripture suddenly slows down and tells us something painfully human about King Rehoboam.
Vayye’ehav Rechav‘am et-Ma‘akhah bat-Avshalom mikol-nashav ufilagshav…
“Rehoboam loved Maacah the daughter of Absalom above all his wives and his concubines.”
Not because this is some ancient royal romance we are supposed to imitate.
And not because Scripture is celebrating a king collecting women as though human beings were trophies.
In fact, centuries before Rehoboam sat upon the throne, God had already warned Israel’s kings against multiplying wives to themselves.
So the shocking number in this passage is not evidence of Rehoboam’s greatness.
It is part of the tragedy.
Because sometimes the Bible tells you what happened without telling you to copy what happened.
Rehoboam had eighteen wives and sixty concubines, yet the inspired writer still pauses to tell us that he loved Maacah more than the others.
Seventy-eight women could not make seventy-eight hearts equally precious to him.
And suddenly this ancient king does not feel quite so ancient anymore.
Because we may not have Rehoboam’s palace…
One more person telling us we matter.
One more thing added to the collection of things we once believed would finally make us whole.
Yet somehow the human heart can remain painfully hungry.
Maybe that is why this verse feels so uncomfortable.
It exposes something we would rather not admit:
You can possess more and still not love better.
You can be surrounded and still be empty.
You can have options and still have no peace.
You can live in a palace and still carry a wilderness inside your chest.
Think about the shadow under which this man grew up.
His father was Solomon—the king associated with extraordinary wisdom, wealth, construction, international influence, and staggering excess.
Yet Solomon himself had multiplied wives on an enormous scale, and Scripture records the devastating spiritual consequence: his wives turned his heart after other gods.
That should make every parent tremble.
Because children can inherit more than our eyes, our surnames, our property, or our mannerisms.
And sometimes what one generation tolerates, the next generation learns to call normal.
That is why grace must do more than improve our behavior.
Because if Christ does not interrupt the cycle, yesterday’s compromise can become tomorrow’s inheritance.
But there is something else buried in this story.
Maacah was not merely Rehoboam’s favorite.
Her position appears to have affected the future of the kingdom.
Immediately after telling us Rehoboam loved Maacah above his other wives and concubines, Scripture tells us:
“And Rehoboam made Abijah the son of Maachah the chief, to be ruler among his brethren: for he thought to make him king.”
What occupied the king’s affection reached into the king’s decisions.
His private preference touched public succession.
The heart never stays completely hidden.
Eventually, what rules inside us starts influencing what happens around us.
What you love shapes what you choose.
What you treasure shapes what you protect.
What you worship shapes what you sacrifice.
That is why Jesus went deeper than behavior.
We often want Christianity to become a divine renovation project.
And Christ certainly cares about every wounded place we carry.
But Jesus did not come merely to rearrange the furniture inside the old life.
He came to make us new.
The Gospel does not say, “Try harder until God can tolerate you.”
The Gospel announces something infinitely more beautiful:
You were a sinner who could not rescue yourself.
Jesus lived the righteousness you could never perfectly live.
He went to the cross willingly.
The answer to the restless human heart is ultimately not another relationship.
Not another person telling you that you are enough.
The answer is reconciliation with God through Jesus Christ.
And perhaps somebody reading this knows exactly why those words hurt.
Because your life looks full from the outside.
But God knows about the empty room inside you.
God sees the compromise you keep deleting from your history.
Jesus knows you cried when nobody was watching.
People think you have moved on.
God knows you are still bleeding from something that happened years ago.
And maybe you have been trying to solve a spiritual hunger with earthly multiplication.

That confession may be closer to freedom than you realize.
Because grace begins where pretending ends.
And Scripture still had to distinguish one love from another.
There is no number large enough to heal a heart that is looking to creation for what only the Creator can ultimately provide.
But before we turn Rehoboam into the villain and ourselves into the jury, remember who his story is really exposing.
Our idols simply fit inside our pockets now.
Some look respectable enough that nobody realizes we are worshiping them.
And that may be the most dangerous idol of all:
the one you can carry into church without anybody noticing.
Jesus does not merely ask what you own.
That is where this ancient scandal suddenly becomes painfully personal.
Not what do you say has your heart.
What could you not imagine surrendering if Christ asked you to lay it down?
Whose approval can destroy your entire day?
What do you run toward when you feel unwanted?
What secret habit becomes your counterfeit comfort?
What are you terrified of losing?
And here is the breathtaking difference between Rehoboam’s palace and Christ’s kingdom.
Jesus gave Himself for His people.
Earthly kings often use people to build kingdoms.
Jesus gave His life to redeem people for His Kingdom.
At Calvary, Christ was not collecting trophies.
He was shedding His blood for sinners.
The crown placed upon His head was made of thorns.
The throne men gave Him was a cross.
The crowd did not shout affection but rejection.
Nails did not ultimately keep Jesus there.
That is the love your restless heart has been searching for.
A love strong enough to confront your sin without abandoning you to it.
A love gracious enough to forgive what you are ashamed to confess.
A love powerful enough to rewrite a life everyone else has already written off.
That is why repentance is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is the mercy of God calling you out of the grave before the grave becomes home.
Maybe your marriage carries wounds nobody knows about.
Maybe you became emotionally attached to somebody who was never yours to have.
Maybe pornography has quietly trained your heart to consume people instead of love them.
Maybe you have been sleeping beside someone every night while your heart has been somewhere else.
The cross was built for guilty people.
Grace is not permission to remain unchanged.
Grace is the power and mercy of God meeting sinners where they are and refusing to leave them there.
And sometimes He begins by tearing away the lie that the next thing will finally satisfy us.
Eventually you discover what generations before us discovered:
A human soul is too deep to be filled by created things.
And perhaps that is the real reason this strange little verse survived thousands of years and found its way onto your screen today.
Not so we could gossip about an ancient king.
So an ancient king could become a mirror.
Rehoboam had more than most people could dream of possessing.
Yet Scripture still makes us look beneath the numbers and toward the heart.
So forget his seventy-eight women for a moment.
What have you been multiplying because one surrendered relationship with Jesus feels too costly?
What have you accumulated because silence with God terrifies you?
What are you using to anesthetize the ache?
This may have hit harder than you expected.
Someone reading the comments may desperately need your testimony tonight.
Do not underestimate what one honest sentence can do.
And think of one person who needs this message.
The friend quietly destroying a marriage.
The woman convinced another relationship will finally make her whole.
The successful person nobody realizes is empty.
The believer who loves Jesus but has wandered far from Him.
Sometimes evangelism begins with something as simple as refusing to keep a life-giving message to yourself.
Because temptation has a strange way of making us forget what conviction taught us yesterday.
You may need these words again.
There is another way you can help this work continue.
Gospel ministry requires people who pray, people who share, people who serve, and people who voluntarily give.
Scripture says giving should come from a heart that has decided freely, “not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
And if Gospel Warrior is one of the ministries you choose to support financially, we receive that support with gratitude, not entitlement.
And whether you are able to give financially or not, you can still help.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.
Test what you read against the Word of God.
And keep Jesus at the center.
Because eventually every earthly collection becomes dust.
Numbers that once impressed everybody become forgotten statistics in somebody else’s history book.
Rehoboam once had eighteen wives and sixty concubines.
Today we remember him through a few lines of ancient Scripture.
And that leaves you with one question far more important than how many wives Rehoboam possessed or which woman he preferred:
If the answer exposes something painful, do not run.
Bring Him the version of yourself you desperately hope nobody ever discovers.
Because the most beautiful thing about Jesus is not that He pretends your scandal never happened.
It is that He can meet you in the wreckage, forgive the repentant sinner, and begin writing something your failure never had the authority to finish.
Your scandal may explain a chapter of your life—but because of Jesus, it does not have to write the ending.
